newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan banks see no early cut in lending rates.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan banks see no early cut in lending rates.

text.p: Pakistani interest rates are likely to fall only if the government keeps its bank borrowing within its budget target in fiscal 1997/98 (July-June), bankers said on Saturday.
Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz withdrew a one percent excise duty on bank loans in the budget he presented on Friday and said this would bring interest rates down by 1.7 percent.
Bankers said the duty was payable monthly, implying a compound impact of around 1.75 percent a year.
"The cut in excise duty on bank loans is a good thing and it will stimulate the economy," Younas Khan, chief executive of Deutsche Bank in Pakistan, said.
He said removal of the duty, which is not part of the lending rate charged by banks to private borrowers, would reduce the overall cost for borrowers.
Pervaiz Shahbaz, treasury dealer at Banque IndoSuez, said the change would ease cash-flow problems for borrowers, but would not induce banks to cut their lending rates.
"It will lessen the burden on the borrowers but the overall interest rate structure may not come down unless the pressure of government borrowing on the banking system eases," he said.
Aziz said he wanted to reduce interest rates from the 20 to 22 percent paid by most industrial and commercial borrowers.
"As a matter of policy we do wish to bring down the interest rate to say, inflation plus two or three percent," he said.
Year-on-year inflation was almost 13 percent in May.
Aziz promised to keep government borrowing from banks to 55 billion rupees, against an estimated 88 billion in 1996/97. The original target for this year was 20 billion rupees.
Aziz's target is lower than the limit of 58 billion rupees set by the newly autonomous State (central) Bank of Pakistan.
"It appears difficult for the government to stay within the limit, but if it does, credit availability to the private sector will improve and lending rates will come down," Shahbaz said.

Bankers said the government's borrowing target looked doubtful given this year's monetary overhang and the challenge of pulling off its ambitious target of raising revenue 26.8 percent without new taxes.
Shahbaz said the central bank should lower its three-day repo rate for banks, fixed at 20 percent in October, if the government wanted to give a supply-side boost to the economy.

He said the government's ability to reduce corporate lending rates by lowering the yield on its six-month bonds, now at 16.50 percent a year, was limited because this might discourage foreign banks from bringing in foreign currency deposits.
Foreign banks now enjoy spreads of two to three percent by bringing forex deposits from abroad, swapping them for rupee equivalent deposits and investing them in government paper.
Bankers say an annual yield of below 15.50 percent a year on six-month federal bonds would wipe out the spread.

"The government might have sensed that the banks will not lower their lending rates, so they slashed the excise duty to ease borrowing costs for the private sector from their own side," the chief economist of a foreign bank said.
